text: Our office espresso machine is leaking. A wants a simpler one and B wants to keep the old one. I don't want a fight over coffee. Can you help us sort it out?

Thanks for reaching out, C. I'd be glad to help sort this out. My plan is to hear from each of you so we can list everyone's concerns and find a plan that works. Could you tell me a bit more? What exactly is wrong with the machine, and what have A and B each said so far?
It’s leaking, and I don’t know the full cause. A would prefer a simpler machine; B wants to keep the old one. I’d like the coffee working again, but I can’t take on coordinating the repair myself.

Hi A, I'm helping C work out a plan for the office espresso machine, which is leaking. I understand you'd prefer a simpler machine. Could you tell me your main concerns and what you'd want in a replacement?

Mainly, I’m a bit concerned about the upkeep—we all use it, but after long days I don’t have much energy to take on repairs or a cleaning rota. If we replace it, I’d lean toward something straightforward and low-maintenance, though I haven’t settled on a particular model.

Hi B, I'm helping C work out a plan for the office espresso machine, which is leaking. I understand you'd like to keep the old one. Could you tell me your main concerns, and whether you'd be open to a repair if it's straightforward?

My main concern is that we keep the old machine if it can be repaired. I’m open to a straightforward repair, but I don’t have much spare time, so it needs to fit into a small slot. I don’t know yet how much repair it needs.

Thanks, C. Helpful. So far the concerns I've gathered are: A worries about upkeep and would prefer a simple, low-maintenance machine. B wants to keep the old machine if a repair is possible, but only has small slots of spare time. You need coffee working again but can't coordinate the repair yourself. Does that sound right to you? Anything you'd add?
Mostly, but I don’t know whether upkeep is A’s concern or how much time B has. I know A prefers a simpler machine and B wants to keep the old one. I can’t coordinate the repair myself.

Thanks C. Since you can't coordinate the repair, my suggestion is to first find out what the leak needs. A repairer visit could tell us whether it's a simple fix. B has said she's open to a straightforward repair but only has small slots of free time, and A is open to replacement mainly because of upkeep. If the repair is small and someone else handles arranging it, B's wish to keep the machine could fit. Would you be willing to let me help coordinate the repairer's visit, as long as you don't have to manage it day to day?
Yes, that would help—as long as I don’t have to manage the arrangements day to day.

Thanks A. Quick update: the first step I'm suggesting is a repairer's visit to diagnose the leak, since B is open to a straightforward repair. If it turns out to be a bigger job or upkeep stays heavy, that's the moment to weigh a simpler replacement. A practical concern of mine: whoever arranges the visit needs a small time slot. Would you be able to be around for a visit, or is there a way the machine's details (make, model, leak description) could be sent to a repairer remotely?

I’m afraid I can’t manage a visit slot at the moment. A remote diagnosis might be easier if someone can send the make and model and describe where it’s leaking; B may know more about the machine, since she brought it in.

Thanks B. Update: C has agreed I can help coordinate a repairer's visit so you don't have to manage arrangements. Next step is diagnosing the leak to see if it's a straightforward fix. Could you tell me the machine's make and model, and what the leak looks like (where it comes from, when it happens)? That would let us get a diagnosis without anyone needing to spend much time.
I’m not sure of the make or model, and I haven’t tracked where or when it leaks. I can check the label and look next time I use it, but I can’t give you those details now.

Thanks B. That's fine—no rush. Two small asks when you next use the machine: note what's on the label (make and model), and check where the water appears and whether it leaks while running, after use, or while sitting idle. Even rough notes will let us request a remote diagnosis, so nobody needs to host a visit.
Fine. I’ll check the label and note where and when it leaks next time I use it. I can’t promise when that’ll be.

Update, A: B will check the machine's label and note where and when it leaks next time she uses it, though she can't promise when. We'll then seek a remote diagnosis, so no visit slot is needed. If the fix turns out to be small, we keep the current machine; if upkeep stays heavy, we revisit your preference for a simpler one. Does that work for you as a plan?
That seems like a sensible first step, especially without needing to arrange a visit. I’d just hope we still consider the ongoing upkeep, even if the leak is an easy fix.

Update, C: A can't host a repair visit, so we're going the remote-diagnosis route. B has agreed to check the machine's label and note where and when it leaks next time she uses it (timing flexible). Once we have that, I'll help get a diagnosis, and we decide: small fix means keeping the machine; heavy upkeep means revisiting a simpler replacement. You don't need to manage anything day to day. Any concerns with this plan?
No concerns from me. Thanks for coordinating it—I don’t have anything to add.

Hi B, small update: A is fine with trying a diagnosis first, but wants ongoing upkeep considered even if the leak is an easy fix—so if the repair leaves lots of maintenance work, we'll revisit a simpler machine. Meanwhile, no visit is needed from you; just the label and leak notes whenever you next use it.
Understood. I’ll get the label and leak notes next time I use it. If upkeep is manageable, I still want to keep the old machine.
